```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(janitor)
library(here)
```

# The first thing I would explore is the distribution and types of variables. I can begin by simply looking at the data with head() or glimpse(). 
```{r}
#| label: looking at the data
final_data <- read.csv(
  here("data", "processed", "final_data.csv"),
)
head(final_data)
glimpse(final_data)
```

# Then I would generate summary statistics for numeric variables (such as maternal mortality  ratio, newborn mortality, etc.) using the summary() function. 
```{r}
#| label: summary stats
final_data |> 
    summary()
```

# To get a better understanding of the limits of these summary statistics, I could randomly remove values of the statistic for certain country-years and then see how the summary statistics change depending on the group of country-years with missing data. 
```{r}
#| label: limits of. summary stats
set.seed(123)

# Choose the statistic to test and the percentage removed in each simulation.
outcome <- "maternal_mortality"
removal_proportion <- 0.20

# Restrict selection to country-years with an observed outcome value.
available_country_years <- final_data |>
  filter(!is.na(.data[[outcome]])) |>
  distinct(iso, year)

n_to_remove <- floor(nrow(available_country_years) * removal_proportion)

# Draw two different, non-overlapping sets of country-year observations.
removed_set_1 <- available_country_years |>
  slice_sample(n = n_to_remove) |>
  mutate(removal_set = "Set 1")

removed_set_2 <- available_country_years |>
  anti_join(removed_set_1, by = c("iso", "year")) |>
  slice_sample(n = n_to_remove) |>
  mutate(removal_set = "Set 2")

removed_country_years <- bind_rows(removed_set_1, removed_set_2) |>
  arrange(removal_set, iso, year)

# Display exactly which country-years are removed in each simulation.
removed_country_years |>
  group_by(removal_set, iso) 

remove_country_years <- function(data, removal_set, outcome) {
  data |>
    left_join(
      removal_set |>
        select(iso, year) |>
        mutate(remove_value = TRUE),
      by = c("iso", "year")
    ) |>
    mutate(
      simulated_value = if_else(
        coalesce(remove_value, FALSE),
        NA_real_,
        .data[[outcome]]
      )
    ) |>
    select(-remove_value)
}

summarise_values <- function(data, value, scenario, n_removed) {
  data |>
    summarise(
      scenario = scenario,
      n_removed = n_removed,
      n_observed = sum(!is.na(.data[[value]])),
      mean = mean(.data[[value]], na.rm = TRUE),
      median = median(.data[[value]], na.rm = TRUE),
      sd = sd(.data[[value]], na.rm = TRUE)
    )
}

simulated_set_1 <- remove_country_years(final_data, removed_set_1, outcome)
simulated_set_2 <- remove_country_years(final_data, removed_set_2, outcome)

comparison <- bind_rows(
  summarise_values(final_data, outcome, "Original data", 0),
  summarise_values(simulated_set_1, "simulated_value", "Set 1 removed", n_to_remove),
  summarise_values(simulated_set_2, "simulated_value", "Set 2 removed", n_to_remove)
)

comparison
```

# I could also use graphs to map the distribution of variables with a logarithmic transformation of the y-values where appropriate. 
```{r}
#| label: Distribution of maternal_mortality and under5_mortality

#distribution of maternal mortality
final_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = maternal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Maternal mortality Ratio (Per 1000)",
    y = "Number of Countries"
  )

  final_data |>#log tranformation
  ggplot(aes(x = maternal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Maternal mortality Ratio",
    y = "Number of countries"
  ) +
  scale_y_log10()

#distribution of infant mortality ratio
final_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = infant_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Infant mortality Ratio (Per 1000)",
    y = "Number of Countries"
  )

 
#distribution of neonatal mortality ratio
final_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = neonatal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Neonatal mortality Ratio (Per 1000)",
    y = "Number of Countries"
  ) 

#distribution of under 5 mortality ratio
final_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = under5_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = "Under 5 mortality Ratio (Per 1000)",
    y = "Number of Countries"
  )


#There are a couple of outliers with maternal mortality values> 1750 per 1000
final_data|>
    filter(maternal_mortality>1750)|>
      select(iso, maternal_mortality, year)
    
#SLE (Sierra Lione) has a high maternal mortality rate from 2000-2005 there likely was a long-lasting conflict during that time period. Should read more on this to confirm

#distribution of armed conflict
final_data|>
  ggplot() +
    geom_bar(aes(
        x=factor(armed_conflict)
    )) +
    labs(x = "Armed Conflict", y = "Count")

#drought
  final_data|>
  ggplot() +
    geom_bar(aes(
        x=factor(drought)
    )) +
    labs(x = "Drought", y = "Count")

#earthquake
  final_data|>
  ggplot() +
    geom_bar(aes(
        x=factor(earthquake)
    )) +
    labs(x = "Earthquake", y = "Count")
```

# This may help identify outliers, which I could explore further for patterns with other variables.
```{r}
#| label: looking at maternal mortality and armed conflict
#Looking at armed conflict and maternal mortality together
 ggplot(final_data, aes(x = factor(armed_conflict), y = maternal_mortality)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Armed conflict (0 = no, 1 = yes)",
    y = "Maternal mortality (Per 1000)"
  )
#The presence of armed conflict seems associated with the highest recorded maternal maortality ratio in this data set
```

# I could look at the variable types using the table() function and see where expected variable types do not match. 
```{r}
#| label: variable type
#Note: opted not to use the table function, instead directly used class() 
final_data |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ paste(class(.x), collapse = ", "))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "class"
  )
```

# Once I am done observing the kinds and distributions of the variables, I would explore the degree, extent, and kinds of missingness, as the preliminary glimpse into the data would reveal that there is quite a bit of missingness in the armed conflict data.

```{r}
#| label: missing data observations
get_dupes(final_data)#checking for duplicate data

final_data |>#look at degree of missingness for each variable
  summarise(
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "n_missing"
  ) |>
  mutate(percent_missing = 100 * n_missing / nrow(final_data)) |>
  arrange(desc(n_missing))

#the same amount of missing values for drought and earthquake- worth investigating
final_data|>
  tabyl(drought, earthquake,  show_na = TRUE) 
#earthquake and drought seem to be missing together
```
